seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 422 HTS Chapter 07 tariff lines — potatoes, tomatoes, onions and garlic, lettuce, peppers, asparagus, mushrooms, frozen and dried vegetables, beans and lentils, cassava. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, filterable by product name.
keywords: edible vegetables and certain roots and tubers tariff

overview.intro:
Chapter 07 covers vegetables — fresh, chilled, frozen, provisionally preserved and dried — plus dried beans, peas and lentils and starchy roots like cassava and sweet potatoes. Most of its **422 tariff lines** carry small per-kilogram rates, and many change with the season: tomatoes pay 3.9¢/kg in spring and fall and 2.8¢/kg the rest of the year, and asparagus flown in between September 15 and November 15 pays 5% instead of 21.3%. A few are high: 29.8% on dried garlic and onion powder, 8.8¢/kg + 20% on fresh mushrooms.

The U.S. imported $14.35B of these goods in 2025, 80% of it from Mexico and Canada, and USMCA-qualifying produce from both enters free. Since **July 24, 2026** most other suppliers pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** on top (EU goods 10% in total, China +37.5% or +20%) — but **91 lines are exempt**, including all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, sowing seeds, cassava and taro. Two **antidumping duties** sit outside the schedule: 17.09% on most fresh tomatoes from Mexico and $4.71/kg on fresh garlic from China.

productGroups.label: Potatoes
productGroups.blurb: Every potato line is 0.5¢/kg. Certified seed potatoes (0701.10) are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; table and processing potatoes are not.

productGroups.label: Tomatoes
productGroups.blurb: 3.9¢/kg from March 1 to July 14 and September 1 to November 14, 2.8¢/kg the rest of the year. No 2026 Section 301 duty applies to tomatoes, but fresh tomatoes from Mexico carry an antidumping duty (17.09% for most exporters).

productGroups.label: Onions, garlic & leeks
productGroups.blurb: Onions 3.1¢/kg (onion sets 0.83¢/kg), garlic 0.43¢/kg, leeks 20%. Fresh garlic from China also carries an antidumping duty of $4.71/kg on top of its Section 301 duties.

productGroups.label: Cabbage, broccoli & cauliflower
productGroups.blurb: Mostly ad valorem: broccoli and cauliflower 2.5% in summer (June 5 to October 15) and 10% otherwise (14% if cut), Brussels sprouts 12.5%, kale and other brassicas 20%, cabbage 0.54¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Lettuce & chicory
productGroups.blurb: Lettuce is seasonal: 0.4¢/kg from June 1 to October 31, 3.7¢/kg the rest of the year. Witloof chicory and other chicory 0.15¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Carrots, beets & other roots
productGroups.blurb: Whole carrots 0.7¢/kg (1.4¢/kg if under 10 cm), cut carrots 14.9%, turnips free, other salad roots such as radishes and beets 1.9% to 10%.

productGroups.label: Cucumbers
productGroups.blurb: The rate depends on the month: 4.2¢/kg December to February, 5.6¢/kg March to June and September to November, 1.5¢/kg in July and August.

productGroups.label: Fresh peas & beans
productGroups.blurb: Fresh peas 0.5¢/kg in July to September and 2.8¢/kg otherwise; fresh beans 4.9¢/kg; cowpeas (other than black-eye peas) free.

productGroups.label: Other fresh vegetables
productGroups.blurb: The chapter's biggest group: peppers 4.4¢ to 4.7¢/kg, squash 1.5¢/kg, asparagus 5% if air-freighted between September 15 and November 15 (otherwise 21.3%), fresh mushrooms 8.8¢/kg + 20%, sweet corn 21.3%, spinach and okra 20%. Jicama, breadfruit and chayote are on the Section 301 exemption list.

productGroups.label: Frozen vegetables
productGroups.blurb: Frozen potatoes, spinach and sweet corn 14%, frozen peas 1¢ to 2¢/kg, other frozen vegetables 11.3% whole or 14.9% cut, mixtures 14%. Frozen French fries are not here: they are prepared vegetables (Chapter 20).

productGroups.label: Provisionally preserved vegetables
productGroups.blurb: Vegetables kept in brine or sulfur water for transport and not ready to eat: olives by drained weight (3.7¢ to 8.6¢/kg), cucumbers 7.7%, mushrooms 5.7¢/kg + 8%, capers 8%.
productGroups.rateSummary: 3.7¢/kg on drained weight · 5.9¢/kg on drained weight · 8.6¢/kg on drained weight · 7.7% · 5.7¢/kg on drained weight + 8% · 5.7¢/kg on drained weight +8% · Free · 8% · 5.1%

productGroups.label: Dried vegetables
productGroups.blurb: Some of the chapter's highest rates: onion powder and dried garlic 29.8%, other dried onion 21.3%, most other dried vegetables 8.3%. Dried shiitake and wood ear mushrooms are on the Section 301 exemption list.

productGroups.label: Dried beans, peas & lentils
productGroups.blurb: Low per-kilogram rates: lentils 0.15¢/kg, chickpeas 1.4¢/kg, dry beans 0.8¢ to 1.5¢/kg, split peas and cowpeas free. Seeds for sowing, Bambara beans and guar seeds are on the Section 301 exemption list; ordinary dry beans and lentils are not.

productGroups.label: Cassava, sweet potatoes & other roots
productGroups.blurb: Ad valorem rates from free to 20%: sweet potatoes 4.5% (6% frozen), cassava 7.9% to 11.3%, fresh taro 2.3%, fresh yautia 16%. Cassava, taro, yautia and frozen or dried roots are on the Section 301 exemption list; sweet potatoes and yams are not.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: 20 tonnes of Roma tomatoes from Sinaloa, entered in January
workedExamples.body: From November 15 to the end of February the rate is 2.8¢/kg: 20,000 kg × $0.028 = **$560**, or **$0** with a USMCA claim. Tomatoes are on the Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86), so no extra tariff applies. What does apply is the **antidumping duty on fresh tomatoes from Mexico**: a cash deposit of 17.09% of the entered value for most exporters (91 FR 33363). At $1.20/kg the load is worth $24,000, so the deposit is **$4,101.60** — far more than the tariff.

workedExamples.title: Air-freighted asparagus from Peru, entered in October
workedExamples.body: Whole asparagus flown in between September 15 and November 15 pays 5% (21.3% at other times), and the Peru Trade Promotion Agreement (SPI **PE**) makes either rate Free. The 12.5% Section 301 duty on goods of Peru (9903.05.63) still applies with an FTA claim (U.S. note 52(a)): a $50,000 shipment pays **$6,250**. Without the PE claim it would pay another $2,500 (5%).

workedExamples.title: Garlic powder from China
workedExamples.body: Dried garlic has a 29.8% base rate. Goods of China add 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31): **67.3%** in total, or $6,730 on a $10,000 shipment. Fresh garlic (0703.20) is different: 0.43¢/kg + 37.5%, plus the antidumping deposit of $4.71/kg on garlic from China (89 FR 48373).

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover forage products of heading 1214.

**Note 2.** In headings 0709, 0710, 0711 and 0712 the word "vegetables" includes edible mushrooms, truffles, olives, capers, marrows, pumpkins, eggplants (aubergines), sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata), fruits of the genus Capsicum (peppers) or of the genus Pimenta (e.g., allspice), fennel, parsley, chervil, tarragon, cress and sweet marjoram (Marjorana hortensis or Origanum marjorana).

**Note 3.** Heading 0712 covers all dried vegetables of the kinds falling in headings 0701 to 0711, other than: (a) dried leguminous vegetables, shelled (heading 0713); (b) sweet corn in the forms specified in headings 1102 to 1104; (c) flour, meal, powder, flakes, granules and pellets of potatoes (heading 1105); (d) flour, meal and powder of the dried leguminous vegetables of heading 0713 (heading 1106).

**Note 4.** However, dried or crushed or ground fruits of the genus Capsicum (peppers) or of the genus Pimenta (e.g., allspice) are excluded from this chapter (heading 0904).

**Note 5.** Heading 0711 applies to vegetables which have been treated solely to ensure their provisional preservation during transport or storage prior to use (for example, by sulfur dioxide gas, in brine, in sulfur water or in other preservative solutions), provided they remain unsuitable for immediate consumption in that state.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Unless the context requires otherwise, the provisions of this chapter cover the named products whether or not reduced in size.

**2.** In the assessment of duty on any kind of vegetables, any foreign matter or impurities mixed therewith shall not be segregated nor shall any allowance therefor be made.

**3.** Articles of a kind covered by this chapter that can be used either for food or for sowing or planting (e.g., onions, onion sets, shallots, garlic, potatoes, and potato eyes) remain classified in this chapter even if rendered inedible as the result of treatment with insecticides, fungicides or similar chemicals.

**4.** In subheading 0701.10, the expression "seed" covers only seed potatoes which are certified by a responsible officer or agency of a foreign government in accordance with official rules and regulations to have been grown and approved especially for use as seed, in containers marked with the foreign government's official seed potato tags and imported for use as seed.

**5.** The aggregate quantity of olives entered under subheadings 0711.20.18 and 2005.70.06 in any calendar year shall not exceed 4,400 metric tons.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 07: Edible Vegetables and Certain Roots and Tubers — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 07 Vegetable Tariff Updates 2026 — Mexico Tomatoes, China Garlic, Section 301 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 07 vegetables since January 2025: unchanged base rates, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and their exemption list, and the 17.09% antidumping duty on Mexican tomatoes — with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 07 base rate changed: 412 of the 422 lines read the same, and the other 10 are new statistical lines for certified-organic produce at their old rate.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35% and Mexico +25% on goods that did not qualify for USMCA, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, vegetables from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**, except **91 lines on the exemption list** (all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, sowing seeds, cassava, taro and a few others). China pays more because its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties stack on top (**+37.5% or +20%**). **USMCA-qualifying produce from Canada and Mexico is still exempt.** Separately, fresh tomatoes from Mexico have carried an **antidumping duty of 17.09%** for most exporters since July 14, 2025.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 07 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemption list, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A, the scheduled Nicaragua tariff, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, and the antidumping orders on fresh tomatoes from Mexico and fresh garlic from China. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods: no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). 91 of the 422 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) and pay no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country: all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, seeds for sowing, cassava, taro, yautia and a few others. The 2025 IEEPA duty on Mexico (+25%, 9903.01.01) ended February 24, 2026. The antidumping duty on fresh tomatoes (17.09% for most exporters, since July 14, 2025) is not a tariff-schedule duty and applies with or without a USMCA claim.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying peppers, cucumbers, squash and asparagus from Mexico pay $0; produce that does not qualify pays the base rate plus 10% of value. A $24,000 load of Mexican tomatoes pays no tariff with USMCA, but a $4,101.60 antidumping deposit.

inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods: no Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). 91 of the 422 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) and pay no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country: all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, seeds for sowing, cassava, taro, yautia and a few others. The 2025 IEEPA duty on Canada (+35%, 9903.01.10) ended February 24, 2026. The 2026 Section 338 duties on certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy and motor vehicles (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) list no Chapter 07 line.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying potatoes, greenhouse cucumbers and peppers from Canada pay $0; Canadian goods that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 10% of value.

inEffect.exemption: 91 of the 422 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) and pay no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country: all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, seeds for sowing, cassava, taro, yautia and a few others. The Peru Trade Promotion Agreement (PE) makes the base rate Free on the dutiable lines but does not remove the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). The IEEPA reciprocal duty on Peru ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Fresh asparagus from Peru claimed under PE pays 12.5% of value: $6,250 on a $50,000 shipment, in any season.

inEffect.exemption: Two Section 301 duties stack. The 2026 action adds 12.5% (9903.05.31, from July 24, 2026) on the 331 lines that are not on the exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)). The 2018–2019 actions add 25% (List 3, 9903.88.03, 281 lines) or 7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15, 141 lines) on every Chapter 07 line, exemption list included. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026. Fresh garlic also carries an antidumping deposit of $4.71/kg.

changes.title: No Chapter 07 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 412 of the 422 lines carry the same General rate in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The other 10 are new statistical lines that split certified-organic Brussels sprouts, Agaricus mushrooms, spinach and frozen vegetables out of existing lines, at the same rate as their 8-digit line. No General rate changed.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover most vegetables
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), except the 91 Chapter 07 lines on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86): fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, sowing seeds, cassava, taro, yautia and others. EU goods pay 10% in total where the base rate is lower; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94); other FTA claims do not remove it.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)) includes 26 Chapter 07 subheadings, among them tomatoes, cassava, taro and yautia. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USITC keeps the antidumping order on Mexican tomatoes
changes.detail: In a changed-circumstances review requested by Mexican growers, the USITC determined that changed circumstances sufficient to warrant revoking the antidumping order on fresh tomatoes from Mexico do not exist. The order and its cash deposits (17.09% for most exporters) stay in place.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: APHIS authorizes fresh glasswort from Israel
changes.detail: Fresh leaves and stems of glasswort (Salicornia europaea) for consumption may be imported from Israel under APHIS phytosanitary measures. A pest risk analysis for fresh sweet potatoes from South Korea (comments closed May 12, 2026) and one for globe artichokes from Sardinia, Italy were published earlier in 2026; no decision notice for either had been published in the Federal Register as of October 11, 2026.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. The product exemption list (9903.03.03) included 26 Chapter 07 subheadings — tomatoes (0702), jicama, breadfruit and chayote, bamboo shoots and water chestnuts (0710.80.15), capers, dried wood ears and shiitake, Bambara beans, cassava, taro, yautia and Chinese water chestnuts; USMCA goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Tomatoes for processing need SC-6 and a certification to stay outside the antidumping order
changes.detail: Commerce clarified that Mexican tomatoes imported for processing (and therefore excluded from the order) must be entered with USDA's Importer's Exempt Commodity Form (SC-6) and a Processing Tomatoes Certification Form, uploaded to ACE by entry summary. The coverage of the order did not change.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025, when it had lapsed. AGOA (SPI D) makes most dutiable Chapter 07 lines Free for listed sub-Saharan countries (the Section 301 duty, where a country has one, still applies). GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua scheduled: 10% in 2027, 15% in 2028
changes.detail: USTR's Section 301 action on Nicaragua phases in a tariff on goods of Nicaragua that do not originate under CAFTA-DR (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028, on every Chapter 07 line, on top of the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty where that applies. Goods entered with a CAFTA-DR claim are not covered.

changes.title: Agricultural exemption from the reciprocal tariff reached 26 Chapter 07 subheadings
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 exempted listed farm products from the reciprocal duties. The list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)) covered tomatoes (0702), jicama, breadfruit and chayote, bamboo shoots and water chestnuts (0710.80.15), capers, dried wood ears and shiitake, Bambara beans, cassava, taro, yautia and Chinese water chestnuts. Other vegetables — onions, garlic, peppers, cucumbers, asparagus, potatoes, frozen and dried vegetables, dry beans and lentils — kept paying until the duties ended on February 24, 2026.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Antidumping duty on fresh tomatoes from Mexico
changes.detail: Commerce withdrew from the 2019 suspension agreement, which had set minimum prices instead of duties, and imposed an antidumping order on fresh and chilled tomatoes from Mexico (heading 0702). CBP collects cash deposits of 17.09% of value for most exporters (2.81% to 273.43% for the named companies). Tomatoes for processing are excluded. The duty applies with or without a USMCA claim.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Antidumping order on fresh garlic from China continued for five more years
changes.detail: After the fifth sunset review, Commerce continued the 1994 antidumping order on fresh garlic from China (fresh, chilled, frozen, provisionally preserved or water-packed garlic, 0703.20 and related lines). The China-wide cash deposit is $4.71 per kilogram (89 FR 48373), on top of the tariff and the Section 301 duties.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of vegetables fell from **$16.52B in 2024 to $14.35B in 2025** (-13.1%), the first annual drop in the 2020–2025 series. Most of it was **Mexico**: $10.24B to $8.34B, a fall of $1.90B against a total fall of $2.17B. Fresh tomatoes, the largest product, fell from $3.76B to $2.96B (-21.1%), and onions, lettuce, squash and brassicas fell 19% to 29%. Canada was flat at $3.16B.

Base rates did not change, and USMCA-qualifying produce from Mexico paid no extra duty in 2025. Two measures did raise the cost of some Mexican shipments during the year: the 25% IEEPA duty on goods that did not qualify for USMCA (from March 4, 2025; ended February 24, 2026) and, from July 14, 2025, the antidumping deposit of 17.09% on most fresh tomatoes. These are values, not volumes, so lower produce prices also show up as a drop.

After the two USMCA partners come Peru (asparagus and onions), China (garlic and dried vegetables), Guatemala (fresh peas and beans), Costa Rica (cassava and other roots) and Spain (frozen vegetables and garlic). 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 07 Vegetable Tariff Rates by Country — Mexico, Canada, Peru, China, Spain | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on vegetables, roots and tubers by country and product group: base rate plus the 2026 Section 301 duty, with USMCA, the Peru TPA and CAFTA-DR applied. Mexico, Canada, Peru, China, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Spain, Ecuador, India, Honduras.
keywords: HTS Chapter 07 tariff rates by country

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on vegetables depends more on **where they come from** than on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

**USMCA-qualifying produce from Mexico and Canada — 80% of 2025 imports — enters free.** Peru, Guatemala, Costa Rica and Honduras claim FTA rates that remove the base rate, but the **2026 Section 301 duty of 10% or 12.5%** still applies; Spain pays 10% or its base rate if higher; **China** pays the most, +37.5% or +20%. Fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, cassava, taro and other exempt-list lines pay no Section 301 duty from any country except China's older lists. The antidumping duties on Mexican tomatoes and Chinese garlic are not in the cells.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-11, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; PE for Peru; P for Guatemala; P for Costa Rica; P for Honduras. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

Antidumping duties are not tariff-schedule duties and are not in the cells: fresh tomatoes from Mexico pay a cash deposit of 17.09% of value for most exporters (since July 14, 2025, with or without USMCA), and fresh garlic from China $4.71/kg.
The rate is not the only gate: APHIS must have authorized that vegetable from that country, and potatoes, onions and tomatoes must meet USDA Section 8e grade rules (see Tariff engineering).
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. Note 52(b) (9903.05.86) lists 40 Chapter 07 provisions — 91 of the 422 lines — exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties for every country: tomatoes, seed potatoes, jicama, breadfruit, chayote, bamboo shoots and water chestnuts (0710.80.15), capers, dried wood ears and shiitake, sweet corn seed, legume seeds for sowing, Bambara beans, guar seeds, cassava, taro, yautia and most frozen or dried Chinese water chestnuts. Notes 52(c)–(e) name no Chapter 07 article, note 52(i) covers CAFTA-DR textiles only, and none of the country exception lists in note 52(j) contains a Chapter 07 line. The Brazil exemption list (note 50(a)(ii)) has 26 Chapter 07 subheadings; the Canada Section 338 lists (note 51) have none. China's List 3 (281 lines) and List 4A (141 lines) together cover all 422.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 07: Edible Vegetables and Certain Roots and Tubers — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Vegetables into the U.S.: Permits, Phytosanitary Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 07) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The USDA, FDA and antidumping rules for each HTS Chapter 07 line — APHIS permits and phytosanitary certificates, Section 8e grade rules for tomatoes, onions and potatoes, FSVP and prior notice — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, the Section 301 exemption list, seasonal rates and FTA claims.
keywords: import vegetables into the us requirements

tariffEngineering.intro:
Before a vegetable shipment pays any duty it has to be **allowed in**. USDA APHIS decides which vegetables may come from which country and under what conditions (permit, phytosanitary certificate, inspection, sometimes a treatment or a pest-free area). Potatoes, onions and tomatoes must also meet USDA grade and size rules, and FDA requires prior notice and a foreign supplier verification program for every food import.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** for Canadian and Mexican produce, check whether the line is on the **Section 301 exemption list**, time entries to the lower **seasonal rate**, and claim the **FTA rate** where one exists. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation. None of them removes an **antidumping duty** — the one exception is the processing-tomato exclusion described below.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on vegetables from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on goods of Canada or Mexico (on the 331 lines not on the exemption list) plus the base rate
levers.appliesTo: All 422 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA — vegetables grown in Canada or Mexico qualify
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. No prescribed form; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the antidumping duty on fresh tomatoes from Mexico (17.09% for most exporters). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Check the Section 301 exemption list before you budget the extra duty
levers.saves: The whole 2026 Section 301 duty — 10% or 12.5% of value for most countries — on 91 of the 422 lines
levers.appliesTo: Fresh tomatoes (0702), seed potatoes (0701.10), jicama, breadfruit and chayote, bamboo shoots and water chestnuts, capers, dried wood ears and shiitake, sweet corn seed, legume seeds for sowing, Bambara beans, guar seeds, cassava, taro, yautia and most frozen or dried Chinese water chestnuts
levers.document: Correct classification on the entry. Seed potatoes must be certified by the foreign government and shipped in containers with its official seed-potato tags (Additional U.S. Note 4); sowing seeds must be of a kind used for sowing.
levers.caveat: The list (U.S. note 52(b), heading 9903.05.86) removes only the 2026 Section 301 duty. Goods of China still pay the older Section 301 List 3 or List 4A duty (25% or 7.5%), and antidumping duties still apply (U.S. note 52(a)).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)–(b)

levers.title: Time the entry to the lower seasonal rate
levers.saves: Tomatoes 2.8¢ instead of 3.9¢/kg; cucumbers 1.5¢ (July–August) instead of 5.6¢/kg; head lettuce 0.4¢ (June–October) instead of 3.7¢/kg; fresh peas 0.5¢ (July–September) instead of 2.8¢/kg; broccoli and cauliflower 2.5% (June 5–October 15) instead of 10%; asparagus 5% instead of 21.3% when air-freighted between September 15 and November 15
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose description names a date window: tomatoes, cucumbers, lettuce, peas, beans, broccoli and cauliflower, celery, eggplant, asparagus and several dried beans
levers.document: The entry itself: the rate is the one in force on the date of entry (or withdrawal from warehouse for consumption).
levers.caveat: The seasonal rate changes only the base rate; an ad valorem Section 301 duty applies in every season. A few windows run the other way (eggplant is 2.6¢/kg April–November and 1.9¢/kg otherwise).

citations.label: 19 CFR 141.69 (rate in effect at time of entry)

levers.title: Claim the FTA rate (Peru, Chile, CAFTA-DR, Colombia and others)
levers.saves: The base rate — up to 21.3% on asparagus, 20% on spinach, okra and leeks, 29.8% on dried garlic
levers.appliesTo: Lines with a Free special rate for the partner (SPI AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG), and AGOA (D) for listed sub-Saharan countries
levers.document: The claim and certification each agreement requires — for example 19 CFR 10.903 (Peru) or 19 CFR 10.583 (CAFTA-DR).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for the country (U.S. note 52(a)): asparagus from Peru claimed under PE still pays 12.5%. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Document tomatoes imported for processing (outside the Mexico antidumping order)
levers.saves: The antidumping cash deposit on fresh tomatoes from Mexico — 17.09% of value for most exporters
levers.appliesTo: Fresh tomatoes from Mexico (0702.00) that will be canned, dried, juiced or made into sauce or purée — not tomatoes cut up for fresh salsa or salad bars, which stay covered
levers.document: The USDA "Importer's Exempt Commodity Form" (SC-6, 7 CFR 980.501) and Commerce's "Processing Tomatoes Certification Form", completed by entry summary and uploaded to ACE (DIS). Required since February 18, 2026.
levers.caveat: Only tomatoes actually processed qualify; the forms must be complete when the entry summary is filed. The 2026 scope clarification did not change which tomatoes are covered.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (fresh vs. provisionally preserved, whole vs. cut, seed vs. table use) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate or the exemption-list status
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the goods. Questions about whether goods fall inside an antidumping order go to Commerce as a scope ruling (19 CFR 351.225).
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

rules.title: Fresh vegetables: only those APHIS has authorized from the country, under permit, with any required phytosanitary certificate, inspection and treatment (permit not needed for dried vegetables or for produce grown in Canada)
Plants for planting (seed potatoes, onion sets, bulbs): written PPQ permit and general restrictions
Seeds for sowing: Federal Seed Act import rules (labeling, testing, noxious-weed seed limits)
Irish potatoes: Section 8e grade, size, quality and maturity requirements, with inspection
Onions: Section 8e grade, size, quality and maturity requirements, with inspection

Tomatoes: Section 8e grade and size requirements (at least U.S. No. 2; minimum size from October 10 to June 15), except cherry, pear-shaped, greenhouse and hydroponic tomatoes; SC-6 for tomatoes imported for processing
Prior notice of imported food, submitted and confirmed before arrival
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer verifies each foreign supplier's food safety
Produce Safety Rule: standards for growing, harvesting, packing and holding raw produce, which foreign farms supplying the U.S. must meet
Food Traceability Rule: extra traceability records for foods on the Food Traceability List (fresh tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, leafy greens, herbs, fresh-cut vegetables)
Antidumping order on fresh tomatoes from Mexico (A-201-820): cash deposit of 17.09% for most exporters since July 14, 2025; tomatoes for processing excluded with SC-6 and certification

Antidumping order on fresh garlic from China (A-570-831): China-wide cash deposit $4.71/kg; covers fresh, chilled, frozen, provisionally preserved and water-packed garlic, not garlic prepared by heat or other ingredients
Country of origin labeling: retailers must tell shoppers the origin of fresh and frozen vegetables

groups.label: Potatoes
groups.note: Seed potatoes are plants for planting (7 CFR 319.37) and must carry the foreign government's seed-potato tags to use 0701.10. Potatoes from Newfoundland and part of Central Saanich, British Columbia are prohibited (7 CFR 319.56-3(b)).

groups.label: Tomatoes
groups.note: Mexican fresh tomatoes are under an antidumping order (17.09% for most exporters) unless imported for processing with the SC-6 and certification forms.

groups.label: Onions, garlic & leeks
groups.note: Onion sets are plants for planting. Fresh garlic from China is under an antidumping order ($4.71/kg China-wide).

groups.label: Lettuce & chicory
groups.note: Lettuce and chicory are leafy greens on the Food Traceability List.

groups.label: Cucumbers
groups.note: Fresh cucumbers are on the Food Traceability List.

groups.label: Other fresh vegetables
groups.note: Fresh peppers, leafy greens and herbs are on the Food Traceability List; which other vegetables may come from a given country is set case by case in ACIR.

groups.label: Frozen vegetables
groups.note: Frozen vegetables still need APHIS authorization (the permit exemption covers dried, not frozen, vegetables). Frozen garlic from China (0710.80.97.55) is inside the garlic antidumping order.

groups.label: Provisionally preserved vegetables
groups.note: Provisionally preserved garlic from China is inside the garlic antidumping order (0711.90.65).

groups.label: Dried vegetables
groups.note: Dried vegetables need no APHIS permit (7 CFR 319.56-3(b)(1)(i)) but must be free of soil and prohibited plant parts.

groups.label: Dried beans, peas & lentils
groups.note: Dried beans and peas need no APHIS permit; seeds for sowing fall under the Federal Seed Act.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 07: Edible Vegetables and Certain Roots and Tubers — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Vegetable Tariffs FAQ: Mexico Tomatoes, Canada Produce, China Garlic, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 07) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about vegetable tariffs: tariffs on tomatoes and produce from Mexico, Canadian vegetables and potatoes, garlic from China, asparagus from Peru, and the HS codes for garlic, onions, potatoes and tomatoes.
keywords: are there tariffs on vegetables from mexico

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing vegetables into the U.S. — tariffs by country, HS codes and entry rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying vegetables from Mexico and Canada — 80% of 2025 imports — enter free: no base rate, no extra duty.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% (EU 10% in total, China +37.5% or +20%), and 91 lines — all fresh tomatoes, seed potatoes, sowing seeds, cassava, taro — are exempt.
Antidumping duties matter more than tariffs for two products: 17.09% on most fresh tomatoes from Mexico, even with USMCA, and $4.71/kg on fresh garlic from China.
Every fresh vegetable needs USDA APHIS authorization for its country of origin, and potatoes, onions and tomatoes must meet USDA grade rules before release.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on tomatoes from Mexico?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on tomatoes from mexico
faqs.answer: No tariff with a USMCA claim, but there is an antidumping duty. The base rate (3.9¢/kg from March 1 to July 14 and September 1 to November 14, 2.8¢/kg otherwise) is Free under USMCA, and tomatoes are on the Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86). Since July 14, 2025, when the 2019 suspension agreement ended, fresh tomatoes from Mexico carry an antidumping cash deposit of 17.09% of value for most exporters, with or without USMCA. The USITC decided on July 20, 2026 not to revoke the order. Tomatoes imported for processing are excluded if entered with USDA Form SC-6 and a processing certification. The U.S. imported $2.96B of fresh tomatoes in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on vegetables from Mexico?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on vegetables from mexico
faqs.answer: Not on USMCA-qualifying produce: Mexican-grown vegetables qualify and enter free, with no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). Vegetables that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 10% of value (9903.05.55), except the 91 exempt lines such as tomatoes and cassava. The 25% IEEPA duty of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026. The exception is fresh tomatoes, which carry a 17.09% antidumping deposit for most exporters. Mexico supplied $8.34B (58%) of U.S. vegetable imports in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on vegetables and potatoes from Canada?
faqs.answer: Not on USMCA-qualifying goods. Canadian potatoes (0.5¢/kg base), greenhouse cucumbers, peppers and tomatoes enter free with a USMCA claim and pay no Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). Goods that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 10% of value (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty ended on February 24, 2026, and the 2026 Section 338 duties on Canadian dairy, alcohol and vehicles do not cover vegetables. Potatoes from Newfoundland and part of Central Saanich, British Columbia cannot be imported (7 CFR 319.56-3). Canada supplied $3.16B in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on garlic from China?
faqs.answer: Fresh garlic (0703.20) from China pays the 0.43¢/kg base rate plus 37.5% of value — 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31) — plus an antidumping cash deposit of $4.71 per kilogram (China-wide rate), in place since 1994 and continued in 2023. Garlic powder and other dried garlic (0712.90.40) is not among the subheadings the antidumping order lists, but pays 29.8% + 37.5% = 67.3%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for garlic and garlic powder?
faqs.answer: Fresh or chilled garlic is 0703.20 (0.43¢/kg); dried garlic — powder, flakes, granules — is 0712.90.40 (29.8%). Frozen garlic falls under 0710.80, and garlic in brine for transport under 0711.90. Garlic paste and garlic salt are prepared foods outside Chapter 07.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for onions and onion powder?
searchedAs: hs code for dehydrated onion powder
faqs.answer: Fresh onions and shallots are 0703.10: onion sets 0.83¢/kg, small pearl onions 0.96¢/kg, other onions 3.1¢/kg. Dried onion is 0712.20: powder or flour 29.8%, flakes and other dried onion 21.3%. Imported onions must also meet USDA grade and size rules (7 CFR 980.117).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for potatoes?
faqs.answer: Fresh potatoes are 0701 (0.5¢/kg): 0701.10 for certified seed potatoes, 0701.90 for table and processing potatoes. Frozen potatoes are 0710.10 (14%), dried potatoes 0712.90.30 (2.3¢/kg), and sweet potatoes 0714.20 (4.5% fresh, 6% frozen). Potato chips, flakes and frozen fries are outside Chapter 07.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for fresh tomatoes?
faqs.answer: 0702.00, split by season: 0702.00.20 (March 1 to July 14 and September 1 to November 14, 3.9¢/kg), 0702.00.40 (July 15 to August 31, 2.8¢/kg) and 0702.00.60 (November 15 to February, 2.8¢/kg), with 10-digit lines for greenhouse, cherry, grape, Roma and round tomatoes. Tomato powder is 0712.90.74 (8.7%); paste, sauce and ketchup are prepared foods outside Chapter 07.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for fresh vegetables?
searchedAs: hs code for fruits and vegetables
faqs.answer: Chapter 07. Fresh or chilled vegetables are headings 0701 to 0709 (potatoes, tomatoes, onions and garlic, cabbages, lettuce, carrots, cucumbers, peas and beans, and other vegetables such as peppers and asparagus); frozen vegetables are 0710, dried 0712, dried beans and lentils 0713, and cassava and sweet potatoes 0714. Fruit and nuts are Chapter 08.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on mushrooms?
faqs.answer: Fresh mushrooms (0709.51–0709.59) pay 8.8¢/kg + 20%, truffles are free. Dried mushrooms are 0712.31–0712.39 (1.3¢/kg + 1.8% air or sun dried, otherwise 1.9¢/kg + 2.6%; dried wood ears 8.3%). USMCA-qualifying Canadian mushrooms enter free. From the 60 Section 301 economies, add 10% or 12.5% — except dried shiitake and wood ears, which are on the exemption list.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on asparagus from Peru?
faqs.answer: 12.5% of value. Fresh asparagus has a base rate of 21.3% (5% if air-freighted between September 15 and November 15), which the Peru Trade Promotion Agreement makes Free, but the 12.5% Section 301 duty on goods of Peru (9903.05.63) applies even with an FTA claim. Peru supplied $472M of U.S. vegetable imports in 2025, mostly fresh vegetables (heading 0709).

faqs.question: What is the tariff code and duty for lentils?
faqs.answer: Dried lentils are 0713.40: 0713.40.20 at 0.15¢/kg, or 0713.40.10 at 1.5¢/kg for lentils of a kind used for sowing (which are on the Section 301 exemption list). Fresh lentils are 0708.90.15 (0.1¢/kg). From the 60 Section 301 economies, non-seed lentils also pay 10% or 12.5% of value.

faqs.question: How much of its vegetables does the U.S. import, and from where?
searchedAs: where does the us import vegetables from
how much produce does the us import from mexico
faqs.answer: $14.35B of Chapter 07 goods in 2025, down from $16.52B in 2024. Mexico supplied 58% and Canada 22%; next were Peru, China, Guatemala, Costa Rica and Spain. Tomatoes ($2.96B), peppers and cucumbers are the largest products.
